item.title: Should you join: Genesis Computing
item.description: Inside the startup that wants to become the data team for every enterprise
item.content:encoded:
✨ Hey there - this is a free edition of next play’s newsletter. This is part of our series Should You Join, where we go behind the scenes on interesting companies. Our hope is that documenting these sorts of details, which never really make it to big publication press releases, can help you a) discover more interesting opportunities and b) inspire you to think creatively (for any of your own endeavors). You can join our private Slack community here and access $1000s of dollars of product discounts here.

Data engineering is underloved. It’s unsexy. Nobody is writing long-form profiles about data engineers as if they were Tom Brady (looking at you, high-profile AI researchers). If you say you’re a data engineer at a dinner with friends, the reaction is usually closer to “oh nice lol” than “wow you’re so lucky and I wish I could be you.” In fact many people, including people who work in tech and at startups, probably could not even describe what a data engineer does!

But perhaps data engineering should get more of the spotlight. Because a lot of what a company knows about itself, and thus a lot of what determines the company’s direction and long-term success, depends on how good their data engineers are at their job.

You can even think of it in terms of simple questions, like:

  • How many customers do we have?

  • How much did we make in Europe last quarter?

  • Which of our loans are most likely to go bad?

Some companies will have clear answers to these. Some companies will have dozens of conflicting answers. Some might not know at all! Each answer depends on data pulled out of a mountain of systems, cleaned up, and joined together by complex rules.

When data engineering is done well, a company can see what’s happening and act on it quickly. Matt Glickman, who spent over 20 years at Goldman Sachs, believes that Goldman’s single firm-wide data platform was a big part of the reason it got through the 2008 financial crisis when Lehman and many others didn’t. And when data engineering goes badly… It can go really badly. One example is what happened to Unity in May 2022, when the company told investors it would lose about $110M that year because of an issue that basically boiled down to bad data engineering.

Data engineering is difficult and there aren’t enough effective data engineers to go around. Today, I’m writing about Genesis, a company that solves those problems with a platform of specialized AI data engineers.

Genesis was founded in 2024 by Matt Glickman and Justin Langseth, two Snowflake veterans who know the problem as well as anyone (better, actually). Customers already include Globe Telecom and a Fortune 100 pharma company, and Genesis raised a $17.5M Series A this past summer. So I sat down with the team to answer questions like: How does the product work? What’s it like to work there? Why will they win? And: why should you join?

The product

The basic goal of a data engineer’s job is making sure the numbers are right. At a big company, particularly in regulated industries, that’s a lot of work. Take one of the bigger projects a data team will ever do: migrating off an old Oracle system. If you want to do this well, someone has to, at minimum…

  • Find every pipeline feeding the old system

  • Figure out what each rule does, and why it’s there

  • Rebuild all of it on the new system

  • Run the old and new systems side by side

  • Check that every number matches

  • Explain every difference to someone in risk or compliance

  • Hope that there aren’t hidden edge cases that the legacy system just hasn’t hit yet.

A project like this takes months, and it comes on top of the daily work of keeping existing pipelines from breaking. “I’ve never met a data engineer who said, ‘Please give me more data engineering to do,’” Matt told me. “It’s a thankless job, it’s a high burnout job, and it’s highly complex.” So big projects wait, or the company hires consultants to do the work.

Most data problems at big companies could be solved, however, if the company simply had a huge and scalable army of smart data engineers to solve them. Genesis is that army.

Genesis AI agents run inside a company’s own Snowflake, Databricks, cloud account or even on-prem. They learn how the company’s data fits together and then actually do the work: like migrations, new pipelines, bringing a new client’s data into the system, or figuring out why a number is wrong.

For one example: Tower Peak Partners is a global PE firm headquartered in London. Before its first fund closed, the partners wanted their own platform covering the whole firm, with compliance built in. Simon Knowles, Tower Peak’s Global Head of Technology, estimated that doing it the traditional way would have meant hiring five to ten specialists for a multi-year build. Instead, the firm used Genesis, and the core platform was live in four months without adding anyone to the team. Tower Peak onboarded its Genesis agent, Eve, the way it would a new employee, and Eve’s first task was compliance training.

“Genesis really stood out because of the founding team,” Knowles said. (He also works weekly with a Genesis engineer who was a founding member of Goldman’s legendary SecDB team.)

There are a few things that make Genesis work particularly well (and set it apart from, say, ChatGPT). One is context. As Justin put it, “data agents are a separate category from coding agents.” A coding agent can read a repo and run the tests, but a data agent has to work out rules that live in a dozen interconnected systems and in the heads of long-time employees if they still work there. Before agents touch anything, Genesis builds what it calls a Context Graph: a map of the company’s systems, its rules, and the reasons behind them.

Verification is another piece. Matt compared human review of AI work to self-driving cars; in a self-driving car you can’t rely on a human to grab the wheel at the last second, because after an hour of self-driving the human has stopped paying attention. With data, “engineers are already letting go prematurely and won’t be able to re-engage in time when AI goes off the rails,” he said. So a key Genesis capability, called Prover, checks the agents’ work certifying everything is correct.

There is also a critical differentiator with respect to security: Genesis is not SaaS. It runs inside the customer’s own systems which matters to highly regulated companies like hedge funds and pharmaceutical companies. And every customer gets FDEs who help get things going.

The big picture

Long term, Matt said, “Genesis will be the data team for enterprises.”

In the short term, the trojan horse to get into these big companies are migrations. Migrations are a great place to start because they have a clear finish line, and companies already budget for the work (but today, they pay consultants to do it).

Part of the case for Genesis is who started it. Matt ran the core quant team (a.k.a. the Strat team) at Goldman Sachs for over 20 years. Justin has been starting data companies since the late 1990s, including Clarabridge (later bought by Qualtrics for $1.125B), and he’s the lead inventor on 51 patents. The two of them then spent six years together at Snowflake, where they built its data marketplace, won five Snowflake hackathons in a row, and kicked off the company’s work on AI. Their 2023 hackathon win was a demo of Elsa, Snowflake’s first data agent, and that inspired the idea for Genesis. “Genesis wins because we have the platform and the people who’ve solved the most challenging data problems,” Matt said.

They left Snowflake in 2024 and gave themselves two months to launch at Snowflake Summit. Margarita joined as COO right as they signed on as a sponsor, and found out the booth graphics were already overdue. She had no design experience, but made the logo, signage, and booth in 24 hours anyway. “I haven’t really stopped since,” she said.

Asked where Genesis will be in 20 years, Justin said “20 years is so far :)” and gave me a five-to-eight-year version instead: “coordinating the data estates of many major companies brings the best of AI and Humans together to do amazing data work.”

Customers today include Globe Telecom, Tower Peak, a New York hedge fund, several Fortune 500 banks and a Fortune 100 pharma company. Globe Telecom says it now delivers pipelines 10 times faster. The pharma company says that for certain workflows, Genesis has helped it “complete data tasks up to 40x faster.” And the hedge fund put it this way: “We would not have been able to do it without Genesis.”

Sales and partnerships are run by Vince Trotta, Genesis’ WW VP of Sales & GTM, Snowflake employee #33 who spent a decade growing Snowflake’s east-coast business and Marketplace before joining. “Data engineers are often the primary bottleneck for enterprise AI adoption,” he said. Vince has also led Genesis’ partnerships with Snowflake and with Databricks, which named Genesis a Validated Technology Partner in June.

The culture

Lots of the team at Genesis, especially the leadership team, came from big companies. Matt, Anton Gorshkov (VP of Engineering) and Margarita Barrera all worked at Goldman Sachs, and others came from Snowflake. So, for people coming to Genesis from larger companies, “this is a different planet,” Anton said. “The biggest difference is how nimble we are and how easy it is to experiment and try things.”

Today, the engineering team is just five people. “We ship up to 1,000 pull requests per week [with that team size],” Anton said. “We also recognize that vibe coding and AI slop are real phenomena, and so, for everything we ship, we hold a high quality bar and don’t just let AI add a bunch of features.” (The company laptops have an image of an F1 car on them.)

Genesis runs on Genesis. The newest member of the team is Gennie, Genesis’ own Chief Data Agent. Powered by Genesis, Gennie works with all teams at Genesis doing everything from helping Finance optimize internal AI spend, helping Matt prepare for board meetings to dispatching work to the Genesis software factory based on customer feedback reported by Sales over Slack.

A company’s general behavior is often downstream of its founders, and the founders set a fairly rapid pace. When Melinda Smith, CFO, first met Justin, he was “managing a double digit number of concurrent AI coding agents working on several brand new features at once.” And Anton said that you’re not so much working with Justin as “around him, where he is some sort of a lightning bulldozer, clearing new roads in days, and you are a slower paving machine behind, making those new roads drivable.”

“Engineers, salespeople, finance, founders, and ops often work on the same customer or issue,” Margarita said. And in meetings, people “are expected to contribute directly rather than attend only to receive information.” Engineering has just one stand-up a day, Monday through Thursday, and handles the rest on Slack.

Genesis is headquartered in New York, with half the team based in the New York area, and the rest spread across the US. The New York folks work out of a swank coworking space called The Malin in NoMad. New York is where Genesis most wants to hire next, especially for marketing. “There’s no better place than NYC to start a B2B AI company, “ Matt said. “Where else can you meet face to face with banks, pharmas, and media companies all in the same day.”

Margarita described people on the team as “quirky, funny, curious, and above all enjoy working outside their usual boundaries. We’re comfortable with being uncomfortable.” Once a year, Genesis brings the whole team together for an all-hands. Matt and Justin recently gathered everyone in Hawaii, where Justin lives.

Should you join Genesis?

If you’re excited by being, as Justin says, “at the forefront of major companies who are living through the AI transition… to agents driving data work,” then I’d strongly consider exploring Genesis’ open roles. They’re hiring across most departments.

Justin says he wants “people who embrace AI and work with AI agents all-in, no hesitation, with a desire to let AI do as much as it can and push it further.” Matt says he is looking for “self-starters who will take Genesis to a place where we wouldn’t have gotten to without them… People who have solved real problems… And AI-pilled enthusiasts.”

Genesis is a place for hungry, ambitious people who want to make full use of all the tools available to them and move really, really fast. And it’s also a place for experienced folks from bigger companies who want to have a larger impact.

Both founders told me they like non-traditional applications. “We want people who can show what they can do vs. sending CVs,” Matt said, and Justin said any creative way of reaching him is great “as long as it’s not an email prompt injection attempt.”

Go explore open roles at Genesis here.

* * *

Thanks to Genesis for supporting Next Play and making this essay possible.

item.title: Breaking into venture capital without a founder or finance background
item.description: how a guy from southern Georgia tweeted his way into venture capital
item.dc:creator: Jack Raines
item.content:encoded:
Hey there - today’s post is a guest essay from Jack Raines, and this is a free edition of next play’s newsletter. We hope free posts like this are helpful - but we think the best way for you to get value from next play is to join Friends of Next Play. It’s a really useful way to discover what’s next: you get a private Slack community with 2,000+ people, private meetups, a great job search tool, interesting project and company ideas, a directory of people to meet, $1000s in discounts on products you really use, and more. All are things we believe will be useful for your life and career over the long run. If that sounds valuable, come join us.

I’m Jack Raines, an investor at Slow Ventures, a seed stage venture capital fund with offices in San Francisco and New York. I also recently published my first book, Young Money: A Field Guide to Wealth and Purpose in Your Twenties, and I write a regular Substack newsletter also called Young Money.

I took an unconventional path into venture that didn’t involve studying CS at Stanford, working on a TMT banking desk in San Francisco, or founding an AI company when I was 14. I’m some guy from South Georgia with no prior ties to the tech ecosystem who broke into venture thanks to Twitter, Substack, and bit of luck, and I’ve spent the last couple of years between San Francisco and New York working in VC. When Ben and the Next Play team reached out, I was excited to share my story and my thoughts on how other outsiders can break into VC as well.

We’ll start with my background, and why I wanted to get into venture, then I’ll discuss my path and how it applies to venture-curious folks today.

A Brief Backstory:

I grew up in Southwest Georgia and played football at Mercer University, where I graduated with degrees in finance and Spanish in December 2019. I didn’t really know what I wanted to do with my life at ~22 (most 22-year-olds don’t!), but I realized I didn’t want to spend the rest of my life in the Southeast.

Mercer wasn’t a target school for big tech or Wall Street, so I figured I could use graduate school to course correct. In my senior year of college, I took the GMAT and applied to a few MBA programs, and I was fortunate to get accepted to Columbia Business School through their 2+2 deferred enrollment program (apply your senior year of college, then work 2-5 years before matriculating).

After ~18 months working in corporate finance (read: editing slides and Excel files from my apartment during Covid), I quit my corporate finance job in August 2021 to work for a financial media startup, Litquidity. I also started writing my own Substack, which has since grown to ~60,000 subscribers. I spent the next year as a digital nomad in Europe and Argentina managing a financial newsletter, selling ads, and writing my own financial markets newsletter and travel blog, before moving to NYC for graduate school in August 2022.

In business school, I was torn between wanting to double down on “media” and pursuing a career in “investing,” so I explored both. While still working for Litquidity, I made a couple of angel investments, including in newsletter platform beehiiv, I interned for Redpoint Ventures, helping them with editorial strategy, I worked on a couple of consulting projects with other venture funds, and I kept building my own platform, before accepting a job offer from Robinhood to help them incubate a new media platform called Sherwood News.

Six months in, I realized that I didn’t want to work in media. I loved writing, having a platform, and sharing my thoughts online, but I didn’t want to “sell content” for a living. I felt like I was too far removed from the action.

I thought venture capital would be more interesting work than media because I wanted to spend my time working with founders building at the cutting edge of the tech scene, rather than writing about these investors and entrepreneurs from a distance. I also figured that my “edge” was distribution. My platform included ~200k followers across Twitter, Substack, and Linkedin. Instead of “writing for a living” for a media company, why not write on my own platforms and use that to help find and win deals instead?

My problem was that I was 27 and on the backside of business school. I panicked that I had missed the boat to make this career jump.

So How Did I Make the Jump to Venture Capital?

Over the prior three years, I had tweeted ~15,000 times, published hundreds of blog posts, interned for or worked with a couple of venture capital funds, and met dozens of VCs and founders, pretty much all downstream of sharing my thoughts on markets and tech online. Starting with the firms I had worked with during graduate school (Redpoint Ventures and Lux Capital), I found more than a dozen firms in my network, and reached out to anyone I knew at those shops to 1) see if they were hiring, and 2) brainstorm the best way to break into the venture capital world as an outsider.

Three issues that I kept running into:

  • Some funds were only looking to hire junior investors with experience working at “AI startups.”

  • Some funds were only hiring “technical” junior investors (read: studied CS at Stanford).

  • Some funds had structured hiring programs for undergraduates and graduate students, and as mentioned I was on the backside of business school.

But what about a highly-curious writer with a Twitter addiction who could still work his way around a spreadsheet? The market appetite wasn’t quite as strong.

Then one month into the job hunt, I got my first break when I chatted with Kyle Harrison, General Partner at Contrary Capital. He hired me part-time to help them both publish long-form research reports and diligence startups. I worked with them for ~two months, but ultimately they were looking for a full-time hire to focus on building their research platform, while I wanted to spend my time on the investing side, so it was back to the drawing board.

And then I saw that Slow Ventures was hiring.

In late November 2024, I was scrolling through Twitter when I saw this tweet from Slow’s partner in New York, Yoni Rechtman:

Three things stood out:

  1. This was a refreshingly honest take on the realities of venture capital when much of this industry is riddled with hype and exaggerations.

  2. They were hiring in New York and San Francisco.

  3. The job description, for the first time in this job hunt, actually kind of fit my background.

From the JD, emphasis mine:

We look for really smart people / over achievers, who are really driven, know a thing or two already about business generally and finance… you need to be super intellectually pliable and weirdly self-motivated.

The easiest people for us to hire: You got a 1600 on your SATs, and played sports seriously (++ for endurance athletes). You went to an ivy, studied economics or philosophy, or computer science – then they went to goldman, or morgan, or bain or mckinsey (or maybe meta or google) … at some point along that line you work up and said ‘hey, I am kinda done with this career track thing / this isn’t all it is cracked up to be, I want to do something more interesting… and I am willing to apprentice myself for a few years to learn what is going on in the wild west’.

Even better, since then you started a blog or newsletter, or twitter, or tiktok (you kids) and have written some pretty interesting opinions about things. You have strong opinions loosely held, you are intellectually honest, open, funny, not an asshole… confident but humble. You show up for the game prepared, and ready to play and have fun…. Oh, and you have failed at something - for real… and know what resilience and grit means.

Do you need to be all those things? Any of those things – nah… but we are looking for people who fit that vibe because that is what we think it takes to crush it at this.

Things I had going for me: college athlete background, recently signed book deal under my belt, and a backlog of ~15,000 tweets and hundreds of blog posts showing my thoughts on financial markets. This felt like a job opportunity I needed to get.

This tweet also had hundreds of likes and bookmarks, I had no idea how long the job posting had been live, and I didn’t want to risk firing off an application into the portal without knowing if it would get read. I also had no idea if Yoni would even see my DM if I messaged him on Twitter, because he had 10,000+ followers and he wasn’t following me.

So I messaged him on BlueSky, the now-left-for-dead Twitter competitor.

Keep in mind that this was November 2024: election season. Twitter, during this period, was just awful political slop 24/7, and a lot of folks, myself included, were testing out BlueSky. Yoni was also testing out BlueSky, where he only had 25 followers at the time.

I figured the odds of getting a reply were higher on the nascent platform, as there was less competition for attention, so I DM’d him there and said I was applying for the job and wanted to chat. I also immediately moved that conversation to email, as I didn’t know how long the BlueSky experiment would last. (That was also the last week I logged into BlueSky).

A few days later, Yoni and I hopped on a Zoom call. A week later, we grabbed lunch, then he introduced me to one of the firm’s founding partners, Sam Lessin. Sam and I chatted for an hour, he asked what I thought of San Francisco. Slow was hiring in NYC (where I lived) as well as San Francisco, and my preference at the time was, obviously, to stay in New York. But I told Sam that if he offered me the job in San Francisco, I’d move out there after the holidays. He invited me out to hang in person the following week, which was my first time visiting the Bay Area (and my first time riding in a Waymo), and a week later, I received the job offer.

One month after that, I packed my bags and moved to San Francisco for all of 2025. Almost two years later, I’m still working for Slow back in NYC (though I still visit San Francisco ~monthly), and I can confidently say that making the jump to the venture capital world was the best move of my career. The caliber of people I’ve met and worked with over the last two years, both within my firm, at friends’ funds, and at different tech companies has been off the chart, and my personal rate of learning has 10x’d since taking this seat.

But that’s enough about me, how do you break into the venture capital world?

First, the easy way:

There are a few “timeless” ways to get into venture capital:

  • Start a venture-backed tech company. Even if you don’t have a meaningful exit, you’ll meet and build trust with investors, you’ll meet other founders, and your network and pattern recognition will be really valuable, particularly when you’re fresh out of the operator seat.

  • Spend a few years working in a hot startup: If you were ~early OpenAI, Anduril, Anthropic, Stripe, etc, every fund wants to hire you because your prior coworkers are their investment opportunities.

  • Study CS at MIT, Harvard, or Stanford. Self-explanatory: you’re a genius interested in tech surrounded by other geniuses interested in tech. Also if you’re doing this, you’ll probably make a lot more money just joining one of the AI labs.

  • Get your MBA (but only at Stanford): I would say an MBA anywhere else, at this point in VC world, is either a negative or neutral signal. But Sandhill Road still loves Stanford MBAs because a lot of senior GPs are themselves Stanford MBAs.

Okay, cool. But what if, instead of being a unicorn individual who was early to OpenAI, or cofounded an “AI for gerbils” business, or dropped out of Stanford to start brokering bespoke data, you studied finance or economics at a good-but-not great school and you realized in your early 20s that, “Man, venture would be cool but I have no idea how to ‘get in’?” You, like me, have to get creative.

The Only Thing That Matters: Deals, Deals, Deals.

This was already true in 2024, but it’s even more true today: AI is rapidly commoditizing all aspects of “junior VC” except for sourcing. AI can make decks, build financial models, create competitive market maps, and scour the internet for any possible datapoint on any and every company faster and better than any “venture capital associate,” regardless of your background at Morgan Stanley or McKinsey.

The only three variables that still matter for us meat proxies in 2026 is sourcing, investment judgement, and fundraising. And if you’re breaking in as a junior, the only way you’ll be able to move the needle is “sourcing.” If you, like me, are pretty extroverted but didn’t spend four years in the banking / private equity modeling dungeons, this plays to your advantage. Funds don’t need “modelers” in 2026, they need young folks who can introduce new founders to the fund that the fund wouldn’t have otherwise met.

Want to get hired by a venture capital fund? Make them believe that you’ll bring them deals they would have missed. This is why so many venture funds hire young Stanford, Harvard, and MIT kids: their classmates tend to start an outsized percentage of successful venture-backed companies. Guess what? You don’t have to spend the years of 18-22 in Boston or Palo Alto to build out a valuable network. Interested in AI research? Start writing a blog about recent tech breakthroughs in the field. Hop on Twitter and join the conversation; every researcher at the big labs is scrolling on Twitter for five hours per day anyway. Like talking to the camera? Press “record” and share your thoughts on TikTok, Instagram, or Youtube. That’s how Claire Zau got hired by Lightspeed.

In my case, my Twitter following (not so much the sheer number of followers as the quality of investors and founders in that following) combined with various essays I’d written over the last few years provided 1) “proof of thought” on how I viewed the world and 2) high signal that I could generate attention which, hopefully, could convert to finding new deals. The internet is full of communities and conversations waiting for your contributions if you have something novel to say. Twitter, Reddit, Discord, Telegram, Substack, Signal, Instagram. If you can contribute useful additions to the conversation, you’ll find yourself building a network in these emerging spaces.

Of course, you don’t have to just “talk about” what’s going on with tech. The nice thing about AI is that it democratized software creation. “Nontechnical” folks like me (and possibly you) can fine-tune open-source models, build our own software, and jailbreak an old iPhone to let an agent swarm run our dating apps and share the results in a Twitter thread, if we’d like. Build something cool and tell the world about it, you never know who’s going to see it.

Even if these experiments don’t land you a job with a venture fund immediately, they will introduce you to folks starting and working at companies in and around the spaces where you’re spending time. Maybe you’ll get a job offer. If you join a hot company, it’s much easier to break into VC later. Maybe you’ll have an opportunity to angel invest. Even if you’re just writing ~$5,000 checks, building a track record that shows you have access to up-and-coming companies goes further than any thought-piece essay ever could. And if you introduce a few of these companies to a few VCs? Well, they’re going to want to hire you or they’ll risk you sourcing deals for a competitor.

How can you position yourself to have access to up-and-coming founders and companies? Pull that off, you’re hirable. Pedigree be damned. I did it with a blog, an unhealthy Twitter addiction, and a propensity to talk anyone and everyone’s ear off whenever given the chance. Maybe you spend the next six months geeking out on AI biotech breakthroughs and start publishing YouTube videos with your findings. The internet + social media + LLMs have democratized so much of the investment game that was previously gatekept, use those tools to your advantage.

What about credentialism?

While some would disagree, “pedigree” is still useful in that it makes it easier for a new party to underwrite you. Most VCs are pattern-matching in their investments, so don’t be surprised that they’ll do the same when evaluating new hires.

Going to a top school or working at either 1) a “hot” company or 2) a “proven winner” like Goldman Sachs improves your odds simply because it shows that you’re a winner, and it’s easier to pick someone who appears to be a winner than doing extra work to decide if someone is a winner.

An acceptance letter to Harvard means you were smart enough to get into Harvard, which is one less thing the firm has to figure out when interviewing you. If you went to Wichita State? Even if you might be smarter than the next kid, how is a potential hirer supposed to know that?

Of course, the right school or starter job won’t get you hired on its own, but a couple of pedigree stamps reduce the risk that you’ll be totally ignored. But that’s where the value of credentialism starts and ends: it gives you a chance to pitch yourself for an opportunity, but you still need to have some substance (ability to find deals).

Is Business School a Good Way to Break Into VC?

Probably not, unless you went to Stanford GSB. I think, 10-20 years ago, the MBA-to-venture capitalist pipeline was robust, but the venture world has grown increasingly tech, product, and network focused, not “spreadsheet and financial brain.”

I went to a very good business school (Columbia). Columbia even has a competitive Venture Fellows program that you apply for access to in your first year of school (I was rejected!) that provides for priority registration in VC classes, opportunities to work with top venture funds on developing investment theses, and experience diligencing student and alumni-led startups. There were ~16 folks in my class (Spring 2024) who were in the Venture Fellows Program. I think 2 (?) of them had VC jobs right out of school.

Most venture funds don’t prioritize MBAs in 2026. Columbia did, of course, give me a much-needed pedigree boost that likely helped my application, but I landed my job by hustling online. If you want to break into venture, you can’t rely on a hiring pipeline out of your university program. And frankly, even if there is one, it’s probably insanely competitive because venture is a desirable field. The easier (and more fun) path is building out your own network and leveraging that instead.

But also if you want to do VC, there’s probably something cooler to do instead.

This is a controversial take as a venture capitalist, but the truth is that venture is a weird job where you spend all of your time meeting with companies, saying “no” 99% of the time, occasionally investing, and then… waiting. Yes, of course, you can still help with getting a key hire across a finish line, being a sounding board for a founder, or prepping them for a new fundraise, but you’re not “building” or “selling” products like when you work for a company.

I enjoy venture. I think it’s a cool job, and it was, particularly for someone coming from the media world, 100% the right career move for me. But I think a lot of folks who “want to do venture” would crush it joining a fast-growing company, and, ironically, doing that for a couple of years would likely make them a better investor, too.

Everything that I said about “how do you break into VC?” applies to “how do you break into tech” as well. Spend some time learning about where your favorite new tech shift is going. Share your thoughts online. Build something yourself, and tell the world about it. Simply “doing the thing” and telling the internet about it differentiates you from 99% of people, whether you want to be an investor, founder, or operator. But for the venture capital game to keep working, we do need more people building killer companies.

If you want to break into VC, build a network, and prove that you can find deals. But if you’re that good at finding deals, it’s worth considering if you should work for one of those companies as well.

- Jack

To follow along or read more of Jack’s work, you can find him on X, Linkedin, and Substack. And you could also check out his new book: Young Money: A Field Guide to Wealth and Purpose in Your Twenties.

item.title: Should you join: Vouched
item.description: Inside the fast-growing startup building the internet’s new identity layer
item.content:encoded:
✨ Hey there - this is a free edition of next play’s newsletter. This is part of our series Should You Join, where we go behind the scenes on interesting companies. Our hope is that documenting these sorts of details, which never really make it to big publication press releases, can help you a) discover more interesting opportunities and b) inspire you to think creatively (for any of your own endeavors). You can join our private Slack community here and access $1000s of dollars of product discounts here.

How do you know someone is who they say they are online?

And what about when the user is an AI agent operating on their behalf?

The first question is hard enough to answer. Verifying your identity online, like when you open a bank account or see a doctor over video, has been a tricky problem for years. But today, we’re living in a new sort of era. Sure, people still act online, but increasingly, AI agents take a lot of those actions for them. And also, increasingly… AI agents do things they shouldn’t.

We’re living in a new sort of world for identity and permissions online now, the sort of world that might need one powerful control plane for ID: both human and agent. So, who’s building it?

The answer is Vouched, the company we are writing about today.

Vouched started in Seattle in 2018, checking IDs for businesses that never meet their customers in person. Today it does this for telehealth companies, healthcare providers, banks, and more, and it’s passed $10M in ARR (growing fast). Since 2025, however, their product has expanded further; now Vouched also has a suite of tools to identify and govern AI agents using your site, tie them to an identity, and determine what they are (and aren’t) allowed to do.

I talked to Peter Horadan, Vouched’s CEO, and other folks on the Vouched team about what the company is building. Why is this so important now? How does Vouched win? What sorts of people are they looking to hire? And, of course: Should you join Vouched?

The product

Vouched’s product today covers three credentials: physical IDs, digital IDs, and AI agents.

The flow for physical IDs is rather straightforward. If you’ve ever taken a picture of your driver’s license and a selfie, then you have a basic understanding of what Vouched is doing on that front. And this remains a big part of the business; physical ID is often the only kind people have, and while we are in something of an ‘AI revolution,’ most people are still doing important things (like opening bank accounts) themselves! So physical ID matters, and Vouched verifies it well.

But physical IDs are not always perfect. One reason is that they’re easy to fake. “Today [most people] still rely on physical IDs, which can be faked for $100 and are cumbersome to use,” Peter, Vouched’s CEO, told me. The other thing about physical IDs is that they show everything at once. To prove you’re old enough to drink, you also have to show a stranger your name, address, and birthday. There’s no control over the granularity of data you provide.

Digital IDs, however, fix both. They “allow you to just share what you want to share - so stop handing over all your PII to a bouncer just to get a beer,” Peter said. “Share your age only!”

Vouched checks digital IDs, too, which come in the format of mobile driver’s licenses that a growing number of states now issue and that people can keep in their phone’s wallet app. If someone has one, they can verify themselves with a couple of taps instead of photographing a card. And if they don’t, Vouched sends them through the license-and-selfie flow. Launching this on the web in 2025, Vouched says, was an “industry first.”

Then there is the subject of AI agents, the newest (and perhaps most important in the long run) credential Vouched helps businesses verify and govern. We’re now living in a world where people use AI assistants for work and for life and for everything; they’re giving agents their usernames and passwords and letting them log in, book, buy, and file things. “Every website is realizing they now have AI agents coming through their login button using the username and password instead of humans,” Peter said. “These sites have no way to tell agents apart from humans, or even to know if a given agent is trustworthy.”

So Vouched has built the control layer for AI agents. Its software spots the AI agents on a company’s site, checks who they’re working on behalf of (if anyone) and what they’re allowed to do. It stops the ones (like rogue agents) that shouldn’t be there in the first place. Vouched’s customers can set their own preferences and controls for exactly how this is enforced.

Say a patient signs up for a telehealth service with a photo of her license and a selfie, or with her mobile driver’s license. Later she asks her favorite personal AI agent to refill a prescription. Vouched can tell the pharmacy’s site that it’s an agent, that it works for her, and that she allowed it to order refills but not change her insurance. An agent that only claims to work for her, but cannot be verified by Vouched as belonging to her, gets challenged or blocked.

This is all new territory for everyone. Time travel back just ten years and tell someone about this whole agent verification flow and they’d look at you like you were crazy. But this is the world we live in and, if Peter and the Vouched team are right, is an extremely important opportunity.

The big picture

“We’re in a new world, from a fraud and identity perspective,” Andrew Stone, an executive at BHG Financial, which is both a Vouched customer and investor (always a good sign!) said when Vouched announced their $17M Series A last year.

Peter described it to me as two changes arriving at once: “Digital IDs and AI Agent Identity. Every workflow starts with identity,” he said. Digital IDs make it easier for a person to prove who they are, and AI agents make it harder to know who’s acting. Vouched wants to be the one layer a business uses to check all of it: the person, their ID, and their agent.

One reason Peter believes Vouched will win is that fraud doesn’t stay in one place. “A fake identity that works on a bank will work on a health system, and now it will work through an agent,” he said. “Most companies still have three separate teams looking at that.” Vouched checks people, their digital IDs, and their agents in one place, across industries.

There’s also the fact that Vouched has been verifying the human part of identities for almost a decade now. While I wouldn’t be surprised to see a flood of new startups solving agent identity and access problems, many of those startups will likely (1) only be doing the agent governance portion and (2) will not have the experience Vouched has in identifying humans. A big part of this working is being able to verify all the way down to a real human, which Vouched can do.

Vouched is also quite early to this revolution. It launched its first agent tools in May 2025, before most larger identity companies had anything comparable. It also gave its standard for agent identity to the Decentralized Identity Foundation instead of keeping it, so other companies can build on it. “We donated it to DIF because open standards are how industries solve shared problems,” Rosalyn Curato, Vouched’s Chief Innovation Officer, said. An open standard is easier for a cautious bank or hospital to adopt, and Vouched sells the product that runs on it.

It helps, of course, to do a great job for your customers. “Vouched is known for DELIGHTING customers and is the partner most people enjoy working with,” Peter said. He wants it to be the easiest option for any company, of any size, in any industry that wants to verify anyone.

Before long, Peter thinks you’ll see identity checks in new places. “I think gone will be the days of CAPTCHAs. Rather than solve this funny puzzle [you’ll] just be told, show us your ID, and because you have to provide that biometric, we know it’s you.” And 20 years from now, Peter believes Vouched will be “the default identity layer that people, companies, and agents use to prove who they are, whatever credential they hold.”

Vouched recently crossed $10M in ARR and grew 80% last year, Peter said. The team raised a $17M Series A in 2025, led by Spring Rock Ventures, and has made the Inc. 5000 list of fastest-growing private companies three years in a row. They have done all of this with a team of about 40 people, all of whom work remotely. Speaking of…

The culture

Fewer than 50 people, all working from different places, accomplishing some rather impressive feats for an early-stage startup (plenty of companies go on to raise a Series B with less revenue than Vouched has now). How do they do it? And what’s it like to work there?

Peter, for one, has lots of experience. He was CTO at Avalara through its IPO, worked at Concur, and co-founded Lockstep, an accounting network he sold to Sage in 2022. “When he sees something in the market, there’s a lot of pattern recognition behind the question he’s asking,” said Windsor Tanner, Vouched’s VP of Sales. “Working with him can be demanding, but in a good way. He consistently pushes me to raise my own game.”

The reason Vouched is remote is you can “focus on the work, not a commute,” Peter said. When live meetings happen, they’re focused on “working through real business issues rather than simply giving status updates. People are expected to contribute, challenge assumptions, and leave with clarity around what we’re actually going to do.”

You will see your coworkers in-person sometimes, though: the company does an all-employee summit in-person twice per year. “There’s something different about sitting across the table from someone you’ve spent months working with on Google Meet,” Windsor said.

One other principle at Vouched is to be willing to act even when there’s some doubt. “We are willing to make decisions before we have perfect information,” he said. “At Vouched, we’re much more willing to test, ship, learn, and change direction if the data tells us we should.”

Should you join Vouched?

When Vouched got started, it would have been nearly impossible to predict the world we’d be living in today. And, yet, here we are: a world where identity verification is more important than ever and Vouched is in an even better position than the day the company was founded.

Combine that with the fact that they’ve got a previously successful CEO with a talented team, 80% ARR growth and more than $10M in revenue… And I think the picture is rather exciting if you want to get in on the ground floor of a startup with plenty of room ahead of it.

When I asked who wasn’t a fit to work at Vouched, Peter said it’s mostly about whether or not you can be effective working remotely. If you “need an office or a manager over your shoulder to stay engaged, or if you treat remote as a reason to go quiet,” he said, you aren’t a fit. “On a team this tight, going quiet gets noticed fast.”

“Vouched is not a place where being smart is enough,” Windsor said. “We’ve had very talented people leave because they weren’t able to turn their intelligence, ideas, or observations into results. You can be sharp-witted… But at some point you have to produce the outcome.”

If you want the pitch straight from Peter: “Software is eating the world, but it isn’t done yet. The next frontier for replacing manual processes is identity.” And Vouched is the company doing it.

item.title: Weird (but useful) questions to ask startups before joining
item.description: surprising questions that can help you learn useful information about a company
item.content:encoded:
Hey there - this is a free edition of next play’s newsletter, where we share advice and under-the-radar opportunities to help you figure out what’s next in your journey. We hope free posts like this are helpful - but we think the best way for you to get value from next play is to join our private Slack community. There you can connect with like-minded people in tech, see curated hiring lists, attend virtual events, and get $1000s of dollars in product discounts, all things which we believe will be useful for your life and career over the long run. Come join us.

Most people do not know enough about their potential employer before they join.

Sure, sometimes that is fine. You join and things are great, and in the best of cases you walk away with millions of dollars in equity. More of the time, however, things range from “meh” all the way to “this was the biggest mistake of my life.” A few weeks or months or years in, you realize you didn’t understand enough about the company to make a great decision about joining.

There are plenty of logic-brained, ‘smart’ questions you can ask to solve this problem, and to build conviction in the business. We’ve already published a list of those. Perhaps equally important, though, at least for you personally, is to understand the weirder stuff about a startup. To get the “vibe.” And that’s what the list we are sharing aims to help you do.

Many of the questions below may not seem obviously useful, but don’t underrate them! It’s easy to believe that all you need to know is ARR and other left-brained stuff but the vibe of the company, the “frequency” of the people at it, can be equally important to both determining your personal experience and, in some cases, determining the overall success of the business.

If you feel awkward about asking any of the questions on the list below, well, you could caveat with an “I know this is odd, but…”

Questions that will help you understand a company’s vibe (and more)

Note: You can ask these questions to anyone during the interview process. Might even be helpful to ask them to multiple different people to get a bigger sample size of the “vibe.” I am writing them as questions for you to ask yourself, but many of them are things you can ask the company directly. I am not going to tell you exactly how you should interpret the answers. That’s up to you.

What are they reading? What are the best book(s) they have ever read? What about movies? There’s a difference between a Fast & Furious company and a Drive My Car company, you know? It sounds crazy but these can indicate different kinds of expectations, people, values. Someone’s tech media diet (i.e. what journalists or columns they are reading now) can also give you a clearer view of what ‘camp’ they fall into on various topics.

What does the team talk about at lunch and/or dinner? If you can, join in on one of these conversations before joining. At the minimum, ask people what these conversations are like.

What do they think is overrated? You can also ask what popular opinions they disagree with.

Who are their heroes? Who do they look up to? Asimov vs. Elon vs. Ursula Le Guin vs. Margaret Hamilton, etc. - you can learn a lot about people’s values and priorities based on this answer.

How do they talk about competition? How do they talk about former employees? Try not asking this point-blank (you may not get honest answers), but you could bring up competition and former employees in conversation and see how they react. It’s honestly not easy to get people to be completely open with you if you aren’t already working there, but… I think that if you can get this information, it can be revealing.

Who are the ‘high status’ people in the company? What are they like, and why are they respected? There are certain people in every company (even small ones!) who tend to have a certain level of ‘aura’ and respect. Knowing who those people are and why can help you understand what matters on this team.

When the company has dinners outside the office, where do they go? Maybe it’s Sweetgreen or maybe it’s some super trendy Michelin-starred place or maybe it’s McDonald’s. You may want to know.

What are the team’s (or CEO’s) favorite YouTube channels and podcasts? Folks in tech tend to spend a lot of time with this sort of stuff. And the media you take in can shape a lot of your thinking and behavior. Is this a David Goggins/hustle and grind sort of company or are all the engineers watching Northernlion play Slay the Spire on Twitch? You might think this is a ridiculous question with no correlation to work but I would disagree, and I think people tend to self-select into these different groups.

What does the CEO think about? What are their interests and goals? You could ask the CEO, but you could also ask the people around them. This matters a lot for the direction of the company.

What are people at the company obsessed with right now outside of work? There are startups where the answer is nothing, because people are in the office 6 or 7 days a week. And there are startups where people will have lots of answers. Either way, you’ll learn something about the vibe.

What are decisions they’ve made that they regret? People who tell you they don’t regret any decisions are lying or ignorant (in most cases). You might also get a non-answer answer to this (e.g. “we regretted doing X but later realized it was the right thing,” or something really insignificant). These kinds of answers alone tell you a lot about the company. But it’s best if you get an earnest, sincere answer about an important decision the company made that it wishes it could have back.

How does the team act when no one is around? By “no one” I mean how they talk when they believe they do not have to perform (e.g. a small group chat with just a few employees). This is admittedly hard to figure out from the jump, but if you can get in a WhatsApp or similar with anyone before you join (or a Slack) and just start having private conversations with people, personalities will surface fast.

If the company failed tomorrow, what would people (CEO, company leaders, etc.) do? Another version of this question is to ask people if they’d quit for $XM amount of money. You’d need to tailor the amount based on the person. You could also ask it open-ended, e.g. ask the person who would be managing you something like “how much money would I need to pay you right now for you to quit?” It can sometimes be revealing to know how dedicated people are and what they’d pursue if not this company.

Where would people at the company live if not here? Lots of people in tech live in SF or NYC purely because of their career. If that weren’t a constraint, where would they go?

What does the office literally look like? What’s on the walls and shelves? Some companies do the early-20s male bachelor aesthetic, some go hyper-performative, and there’s lots in between. You might learn something about what it’s like to work there, and what kind of people they are in general.

Does the team play games (video or board) together? If so, which ones? A startup with karaoke nights is different from a Starfield company, or a Catan company. (Okay, these can sometimes all be the same company, but not usually, at least not with a smaller team.) You can also ask this question within teams. On the surface level it can tell you where the company sits on a ‘nerdy to normie’ type of scale. But there are deeper insights you might be able to glean from this, too.

How physically fit is the team? What exercise do they do? Sedentary vs. active, jiu jitsu vs. basketball, etc. - I’m not going to pretend to know exactly how this extrapolates but it may be useful information.

You may not get the chance to ask or answer all of these questions. And you may not know how to interpret all of this information, at least not in the way you’d know how to interpret a standard metric like ARR. But learning this information does start to form a layer of knowledge in your mind, however nebulous, about what kinds of people work at the company and how they behave. A sort of information far more difficult to define, but perhaps more important for your long term happiness, than ARR.

(If you want to meet people who are vibes-aligned - check out Friends of Next Play.)

item.title: What you should know before selling your equity
item.description: ideas that are both true and useful as you make this very big decision
item.content:encoded:
Hey there - this is a free edition of next play’s newsletter, where we share advice and under-the-radar opportunities to help you figure out what’s next in your journey. We hope free posts like this are helpful - but we think the best way for you to get value from next play is to join our private Slack community. There you can connect with like-minded people in tech, see curated hiring lists, attend virtual events, and get $1000s of dollars in product discounts, all things which we believe will be useful for your life and career over the long run. Come join us.

There are some topics in life that everyone wants to have an opinion on. Like who you should date. How you should organize your wedding. Whether you should have kids, and how you should raise them. What you should do for a living. And, if you have been fortunate enough to receive equity in a company that eventually becomes valuable, you will know that everyone and their financial advisor has an opinion on how you should think about selling your equity.

Because, as it turns out, even success in startupland is complicated, and selling your equity brings up a number of questions that people would like to help you answer. (Often in exchange for some amount of money from you.) And while there are rigorous guides and step-by-step processes out there on the internet you can follow, I am not going to give you one today, because I don’t know you. I can’t tell you exactly what process you should follow if you are considering selling your equity, nor can I tell you how to make a decision. And I think you should be suspicious claiming to be able to do that on such little information.

Instead, I am going to approach this in the same way I would approach giving travel advice to someone: I am going to share a number of ideas I believe to be both true and useful, and I will let you decide how these ideas factor into your overall plan. Selling your equity is one of the most consequential decisions you may make in your career; don’t let me make it for you.

Thanks to Harvest for making this essay possible. Harvest is a small team of experienced startup folks who will give you a free estimate of your equity’s value (based on their private data and other factors) and show you your options for selling when you’re ready. Of course use your own judgement before making any financial/tax/legal decisions and talk to professionals for assistance. This essay is not a recommendation for you to use any particular service or make any particular decisions.

9 useful ideas as you consider selling your equity

1/ You can be bullish and still de-risk. There’s a weird amount of false dilemma-ism in startup equity where people feel as though, if they are bullish on the potential of their company, they should not sell anything. But it’s worth considering that any company can fail and any company can lose value; most do, with time. Consider the full range of outcomes. For example, you could ask yourself: “If I sold 20% today and the company 3X’d in value, how upset would I be?” and compare that to something like “If I sold 0% and the company failed, how upset would I be?”

Remember that your chances of perfectly timing the market are near zero, and consider that your own experience at the company is likely biasing you in some way. I can’t tell you what to do, but I can suggest that you think about the long term and look at all the possible outcomes.

2/ Ask yourself what you will actually do with the money. It’s often helpful for people to think about what they would really do with all the money they stand to make. How would your lifestyle be different? What would you buy? What new decisions would you have to make with this new influx of money? Little things can make your life a lot better, yes, but a more expensive lifestyle can cause more headaches. And the pure logistics of receiving a lot of money all at once can be a headache on its own. If you can, go in with a clear plan before you sell anything. If you are bullish and you realize your life would not change very much with the extra money, for instance, perhaps you decide to sell less than you would have otherwise (and vice versa).

3/ Taking some money off the table can enable you to take more risks overall. Selling equity tends to be equated with de-risking or risk-averse behavior, but I’d argue the opposite: doesn’t selling equity give you more cushion to take risks? Widen your aperture and think about other risks you might be able to take in life if you had a larger financial cushion. Perhaps you could start up some high-upside side projects. Or you could take a year off work. Or you could quit your company and join a new seed-stage startup that looks promising. Or you could start investing and participating in business ventures that otherwise would’ve been too risky. Think about how ‘de-risking’ may really help you become more risky (in a good way)!

Also, remember: even founders usually take money off the table. And VCs definitely do. It’s not bearish to sell. You are simply doing what almost everyone already does. And you have no obligation to hold your money in the company for as long as possible; do what you want.

4/ Can you afford to not have the money? So much of ‘selling your equity’ advice lives on finance charts in the world of hypotheticals. But what about your real life? Do you have an expensive house you need to pay off? Do you envision an expensive future? Do you need the money? It doesn’t matter how bullish you are about a company if you need (or think you will need) the money. If the money is there, and you think you will need the money… Try not to get too wrapped up in what it ‘could be’ worth someday. Think about your real-life priorities.

5/ It’s helpful to make a spreadsheet. Sure, your financial advisor, if you have one, will probably make you a spreadsheet. But I think it’s useful for you to make your own personal sheet as well. Do a bit of manual Excel monkeying and run the numbers yourself. In many ways this is useful in the way that writing your opinions down is useful: it can help you clarify your opinions and visualize things in a way that nebulous ideas in your head cannot.

6/ Before you make a decision, write a memo. Once you have considered all of the above and perhaps created a spreadsheet of your own, I’d encourage you to write a memo explaining why you are making the decision you are making. Try to keep it under one page long. If you find it difficult to write this memo I would try forcing yourself to do it by setting a timer and a requirement to be done with a draft of the menu by the time the timer goes off.

Why a memo? It’s easy to have half-formed ideas and excitement in your head. It’s harder to ignore a half-formed or underbaked idea when it’s written on the page. If you have people in your life who you’re okay sharing this information with, I would also encourage you to share your written memo with them to get their reactions. Note that you do not have to listen to their advice (they probably know less than you do!), but listening to their reactions can be helpful to calibrate. Maybe you are thinking about this incorrectly. Go in with an open mind.

7/ What’s the worst thing that could happen? People sometimes get so stuck in the minutiae of it all that selling becomes a very stressful topic rather than one to feel fortunate and excited about. Remember that if you are in a position where you can sell your equity for any amount of money, you have far outperformed most people who join startups. And if this still doesn’t comfort you, I’d consider what the worst possible outcome is. In most cases it is your company failing (or decreasing a lot in value), and you not being able to sell your equity for as much as you’d like. And, again… That’s simply the outcome 90%+ of people in startups already experience, and the outcome you likely accepted as the default when you joined the company. It’s not that bad. It’s not the end of the world. You don’t need to stress that much.

8/ You may want to get a really good tax person. Beyond your startup failing, the second-worst outcome of selling your equity, might be selling it but really screwing up the whole tax portion. Which could be both stressful and disappointing; it can also be easy to do, because the tax portion of selling your equity is complicated and personal. It is almost always worth hiring a good tax person to help you figure out the most optimal way to approach this. I would aim to hire someone who has helped people sell their equity before. Not every CPA is familiar with the intricacies of startup equity, and a mistake can cost $10,000s or $100,000s. (If you know people who have been through the process, ask them who they worked with.)

9/ It’s good to donate to charity. It can be a bit sad to see people make a dragon’s hoard of wealth and start penny-pinching and using it to their maximal personal gain. (Sometimes these are the same people who, before this influx of wealth, said that if they were rich one day they would donate to charity.) Sure, you earned the money, at least kind of. And sure, if it’s a lot of money, you probably have a lot of things to buy and a lot of lifestyle changes to make.

But consider that this is effectively “free money”. If you were being realistic when you joined the company, then you knew you would probably not walk away with hundreds of thousands or millions of dollars in equity. And now you are. So ask yourself whether you could part with some portion of it and use that money to help people who are less fortunate. Is your life really going to be that different if you dedicate some % of the money to charity, or if you don’t? I’m not so sure.

You should also consider donating the shares themselves instead of selling first and giving away the cash. If you sell, you pay capital gains tax on the growth, and only what’s left goes to charity. If you donate the stock directly, either to a charity or to a donor-advised fund (which gets you the deduction now and lets you pick charities later), neither you nor the charity pays that tax. You can generally also deduct the full market value if you’ve held the shares for more than a year. If your stock is worth $100k and you paid $10k for it, that can mean roughly $18k more going to the cause.

There are so many charities in the world. Choose which suits you best! There are also plenty of studies and organizations out there which do their best to figure out how effective certain charities are; you could explore those metrics to help you decide if you’re having a hard time.
